transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in today. What brings you here — is there something specific you'd like to talk about or get help with?

Well, thank you for taking the time. I, um... I guess I’m here because things have gotten to a point where I just don't know how to navigate my professional environment anymore. I’m a music director and a composer—I finished my graduate studies a little while back—and, well, it really all traces back to this one major commission I had. It was a highly significant piece, a lot of eyes on it, a really big step for my career. 

But for almost two years now, ever since that commission, I’ve been completely unable to shake this absolute certainty that a few specific people in the ensemble have been quietly trying to undermine my work. And I know how that might sound to someone outside the music world, but it’s all in the subtleties, you know? It’s not like they’re standing up and shouting at me or refusing to play. It’s the constant, sudden schedule changes that completely disrupt our momentum right before a crucial run-through. It’s the seating choices—which, acoustically, completely alter the balance and the counterpoint of the score I wrote, and they know that because they’re highly trained professionals. And it’s these little, calculated comments they make during rehearsals, just tiny remarks meant to subtly question my interpretation or throw off my authority on the podium. 

And the most frustrating part, the part that really makes it impossible to deal with, is that whenever I try to address it, they always have some sort of "proof" that it's completely innocent. If I bring up a schedule change, they’ll immediately forward me some email thread from the venue administration that supposedly explains it, or they'll show me some logistical notes about why the seating had to be adjusted for stage dimensions or union break rules. They always have these emails or notes ready to go to supposedly explain it all away as standard administrative stuff. But I know what's really going on. It’s been nearly two years of this, and it just wears you down, trying to lead an ensemble when you know exactly what they're doing behind the scenes.
Have you ever noticed things happening that you know others don’t seem to see or hear, or have you ever questioned whether your perception of what’s happening might not be accurate?

See or hear things? Like... like hallucinations? No, no, definitely not. I mean, obviously, as a composer and a director, my auditory perception is extremely highly trained. I hear things other people don't notice, sure, but I'm talking about, you know, a slight intonation issue in the second violins, or a harmonic clash that wasn't resolved properly in the brass, or someone coming in a microsecond behind the conductor's downbeat. I hear *that*, but that's just because I have a highly developed ear from years of intensive graduate study and score analysis. I'm not hearing voices or seeing things that aren't physically in the room, if that's what you're getting at. Everything I'm talking about—the subtle smirks they exchange, the way they deliberately drag their feet when setting up the stands to eat into rehearsal time, the very real acoustic dead zones they create when they shift their chairs out of the designated arc—that is all physically, objectively happening right in front of me. 

And as for questioning my perception... I mean, honestly? No. I really don't. Because, you have to understand, my entire career, my entire life's work, is completely built on trusting my perception. When I'm on the podium, if I doubt my read of the room or my interpretation of the score for even a fraction of a second, the whole ensemble falls apart. You have to have absolute conviction to lead. 

Plus, I've spent so much time analyzing these interactions. I go over the rehearsal tapes—because I record my rehearsals for reference, which is standard practice, of course, to check balances and pacing—and when I listen back, I can hear the exact moments they decide to drag the tempo just to see if I'll catch it, or when they intentionally misinterpret a dynamic marking. So, no, I don't question if my read on the situation is accurate. I know I'm accurate. It's just that they are very, very good at masking it. They dress it up to look like normal, everyday workplace friction to anyone who isn't paying close attention. But I am paying attention. I have to, or else they'd completely ruin the integrity of the performances.

Have you ever experienced a time when you felt your abilities, influence, or importance were significantly greater than they actually were—like you had a special mission, unique insight, or were meant for something extraordinary?

I... well, no. I mean, I don't think I have a "special mission" or anything like that, not in the way you're describing. I'm a composer and a music director. My importance is exactly what it is—it's defined by the score I've written and the ensemble I'm leading. It's not some grandiose delusion of being a savior or having supernatural insight. 

I mean, yes, I have unique insight, but that's just a byproduct of my training and my talent. When you spend six years in a rigorous graduate program analyzing the contrapuntal techniques of Bach and the orchestration of Mahler, you develop a level of insight that the average person doesn't have. You start to see the architecture of sound in a way that feels almost instinctual, but it's entirely grounded in study and practice. So, if I'm standing in front of an orchestra and I know exactly how a particular phrasing needs to be executed to achieve the emotional climax of a piece, that's not me thinking I'm meant for something "extraordinary" in a cosmic sense. That's just me doing my job at a high level.

And as for influence... my influence is strictly musical. It's confined to the podium. I don't think I'm influencing world events or, I don't know, controlling people's minds. My goal is just to realize the music as it was intended, as I wrote it. The problem isn't that I think I have too much influence; the problem is that these specific individuals in the ensemble are actively trying to undermine the legitimate influence I *do* have as their director. They want to strip away that authority. So, no, I don't have these feelings of being greater than I am. I just want to be allowed to be exactly who I am, and do the work I'm trained to do, without this constant, exhausting sabotage.

Have you ever experienced a period of time when you felt unusually energetic, extremely confident, or unusually irritable — where you were sleeping less but still felt rested, or felt like you had more ideas than usual, or were doing or saying a lot more than usual?

I mean... no, not really. I don't have these sudden, inexplicable bursts of energy where I don't need to sleep, if that's what you mean. Honestly, sleep is incredibly important to me, especially when I'm in the middle of a rigorous rehearsal cycle. If I don't get my standard seven or eight hours, my cognitive function—specifically my ability to track multiple contrapuntal lines simultaneously and accurately judge intonation across fifty different instruments—really starts to suffer. So I'm definitely not one of those people who stays up for three days straight composing a symphony in some sort of manic frenzy. That's just a romanticized Hollywood myth about composers, anyway. My creative process is very methodical, very disciplined. It's not a sudden, overwhelming rush of uncontrollable ideas; it's sitting at the piano or with a blank score for hours, meticulously working out voice leading and harmonic progressions. 

And as for being unusually irritable or extremely confident... well, sure, I get irritable, but not out of nowhere, and certainly not without a very good reason. I get irritable when, for example, the first chair cellist decides to completely ignore my bowing markings for the third rehearsal in a row. Which, as I was explaining earlier, is just one small part of this whole coordinated effort they have going on to undermine the performance and test my authority. Anyone would be irritable in that situation, wouldn't they? It’s a completely rational, proportionate response to a deeply frustrating, ongoing hostility in my workplace. It’s not some random mood swing. 

And if it seems like I'm talking a lot or saying more than usual during rehearsals, it's simply because I *have* to. I have to constantly articulate and defend my artistic vision to keep them from derailing it. Just last week, I had to spend nearly twenty minutes breaking down exactly why we were taking a specific developmental section at 112 beats per minute instead of 120, because they were subtly, intentionally pushing the tempo to make the transition feel rushed and clumsy. If I don't over-communicate, if I don't explain every single detail, they use the ambiguity against me. So, no, I don't have these periods of unnatural energy or racing thoughts. I'm just a professional trying to hold my ensemble together while they actively try to pull it apart.
